# Lead-Time Reduction Plan: From 14 Weeks Toward 6–8 Without Weakening Quality

## Executive view

The eight-week competitive gap is unlikely to consist of eight weeks of productive work. It is more likely hidden in:

- Order-entry and engineering queues
- Batch scheduling and campaign rules
- Material shortages discovered too late
- Supplier lead times and incoming inspection
- Jobs waiting between operations
- Limited availability of certified inspectors
- Documentation or nonconformance holds
- Rework caused by defects created upstream
- Finished units waiting for final release or shipment

The earlier compression attempt appears to have removed elapsed time by overriding controls, increasing lot movement, or rushing work through inspections. This plan takes a different route: **remove waiting, variability, and avoidable rework while keeping every certified quality gate intact**.

A sensible ambition would be:

- **Within 30 days:** establish factual sources of lead time and stop avoidable administrative delay.
- **Within 90 days:** quote 9–10 weeks for qualifying products or configurations.
- **Within six months:** quote 7–8 weeks for a defined high-volume product family.
- **Within 9–12 months:** approach 6 weeks for suitable standard and configure-to-order products, while retaining differentiated lead times for engineered or high-risk orders.

The company need not force every order into the competitor’s six-week promise. It needs a credible, reliable fast lane covering enough demand to stop losing delivery-sensitive deals.

---

# 1. Establish where the 14 weeks actually go

## 1.1 Measure order-to-ship time at transaction level

For the last 50–100 completed orders in each major product family, reconstruct timestamps for:

1. Customer order receipt
2. Commercial and technical clarification
3. Credit and contract approval
4. Configuration freeze
5. Engineering release
6. Bill-of-material release
7. Material availability
8. Production scheduling
9. Production start
10. Each manufacturing operation
11. Each quality inspection request
12. Inspector response and completion
13. Nonconformance disposition
14. Final test
15. Documentation completion
16. Certified release
17. Packing and shipment

For each interval, distinguish:

- Actual processing or touch time
- Queue time
- Material waiting
- Capacity waiting
- Inspection waiting
- Rework
- Approval waiting
- Customer-caused waiting
- Planned scheduling buffers

The analysis should use ERP, manufacturing execution, quality, supplier, and shipping timestamps rather than retrospective estimates. Informal interviews will help explain the data, but should not replace it.

### Likely finding

A 14-week quoted lead time may contain only two to four weeks of actual fabrication, assembly, testing, and inspection. If so, the opportunity lies in synchronizing work rather than accelerating physical operations.

---

## 1.2 Build a product-family value-stream map

Lead time should be mapped separately for:

- Standard repeat products
- Configured products using approved options
- Engineer-to-order products
- Products requiring special materials or customer witness points
- Products with unusually demanding regulatory requirements

A single average will obscure the opportunity. Standard products may be capable of six weeks, while genuinely engineered products may require ten or more.

For each family, show:

- Median and 80th/90th-percentile elapsed time
- Actual touch time
- Queue at every work center
- Work-in-process inventory
- First-pass yield
- Inspection duration and inspection waiting
- Supplier lead time and delivery reliability
- Rework and nonconformance duration
- Schedule changes and expedites
- Percentage of orders released with incomplete information
- Difference between quoted and actual delivery

The 80th percentile is especially useful. Quoted lead time should be short, but it should also be dependable.

---

## 1.3 Examine the critical path, not departmental averages

Production may appear efficient while orders spend days waiting to enter large batches. Quality may complete an inspection quickly after receiving a valid request, yet the inspection could be requested only after the job has already stopped. Sales may blame operations for lateness while accepting incomplete or nonstandard orders.

The diagnostic should therefore identify, order by order:

- Which event set the shipment date
- Which waiting interval was longest
- How often the same constraint recurred
- Whether the delay was predictable at order acceptance
- Whether expediting one order delayed several others
- Whether quality found defects or merely revealed them

This tends to make the functional argument less important: the unit of analysis becomes the customer order rather than the department.

---

# 2. Set differentiated lead-time promises

A universal six-week quotation would recreate the previous failure. Instead, introduce three order lanes.

| Order lane | Typical content | Initial target | Mature target |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Fast | Standard products, approved options, available materials, no special witness requirements | 8–9 weeks | 6 weeks |
| Configured | Approved modular configuration with limited engineering | 9–10 weeks | 7–8 weeks |
| Engineered | New design content, special materials, customer approvals, or unusual certification | Order-specific | Reduce from current baseline |

Sales should receive a rules-based capable-to-promise tool that considers:

- Product family
- Configuration complexity
- Material availability
- Current bottleneck load
- Supplier commitments
- Required inspection and test capacity
- Customer witness points
- Engineering content
- Requested documentation

A six-week promise should be available when the order fits the lane—not through executive expediting.

---

# 3. Remove time from the process

## 3.1 Order entry and engineering release

### Typical sources of delay

- Incomplete specifications
- Repeated handoffs between sales and engineering
- Custom options sold without review
- Serial commercial, technical, and quality approvals
- Bills of material released in large batches
- Late customer changes
- Manual document creation

### Changes

1. **Create a complete-order checklist.**  
   The clock begins only when mandatory commercial, technical, regulatory, and quality information is present.

2. **Preapprove standard configurations.**  
   Develop a controlled library of approved products, options, drawings, routings, test plans, and certification requirements.

3. **Move approvals in parallel.**  
   Credit, technical, quality-plan, and material-risk checks can often proceed simultaneously.

4. **Set rapid engineering-release service levels.**  
   For example:
   - Standard order: same day
   - Approved configuration: two business days
   - Engineered order: planned after design review

5. **Freeze configuration at an agreed point.**  
   Late changes should trigger a documented lead-time and price adjustment.

6. **Use modular product architecture.**  
   Standardize interfaces and delay selection of customer-specific modules until late in assembly.

This may remove several days or weeks without changing manufacturing speed.

---

## 3.2 Production flow and work-in-process

### Typical sources of delay

- Large economic batches
- Monthly or weekly campaign scheduling
- Too much work released to the floor
- Orders waiting behind low-priority work
- Frequent priority changes
- Functional layouts requiring transport and queuing
- Imbalanced assembly and test capacity

### Changes

1. **Limit work-in-process release.**  
   Release orders according to bottleneck capacity and material readiness, not merely because an order exists.

2. **Schedule the true constraint.**  
   Establish a finite-capacity schedule around the work center, test cell, engineering resource, or certified inspection stage that determines throughput.

3. **Freeze a short production window.**  
   A one- or two-week frozen schedule can prevent daily sales expedites from destabilizing all orders. Exceptions should be rare and economically justified.

4. **Reduce transfer batch sizes.**  
   Move completed subassemblies to the next operation rather than waiting for an entire large batch, where certification and traceability permit.

5. **Create product-family cells.**  
   Co-locate equipment, tools, materials, production personnel, and quality support for the high-volume family.

6. **Use standard work and takt-based balancing.**  
   Document the sequence, expected duration, quality checks, and escalation route for each operation.

7. **Apply quick-changeover methods.**  
   Externalize setup tasks, pre-stage tools, and standardize fixtures to make smaller batches economically practical.

8. **Protect bottleneck uptime.**  
   Prioritize preventive maintenance, trained backup operators, tool availability, and material kits at the constraint.

9. **Stop indiscriminate expediting.**  
   Track every override. Expedites often appear to help the selected customer while lengthening average lead time and increasing errors.

The objective is controlled, visible flow—not maximum local utilization. A machine or inspector occasionally waiting may be less costly than every order waiting.

---

## 3.3 Material and inventory strategy

A six-week customer lead time is difficult if critical components have eight- or twelve-week replenishment times. Some risk may need to be moved from customer lead time into carefully chosen inventory or supplier commitments.

### Inventory segmentation

Classify components by:

- Supplier lead time
- Demand frequency and predictability
- Commonality across products
- Unit value
- Obsolescence risk
- Quality criticality
- Supply disruption risk

Use different policies:

### Stock common, stable components

Hold controlled buffers for high-usage items shared across product families, particularly where supplier lead time exceeds the customer promise.

### Postpone configuration

Stock generic platforms, frames, housings, control modules, or semi-finished assemblies and add customer-specific features after order receipt.

### Avoid speculative stock for unique items

Continue purchasing rare or expensive engineered components to order, and quote those products accordingly.

### Create complete material kits

Do not release an order to production unless critical materials, approved substitutes, drawings, tooling, and inspection plans are available. Partial starts usually inflate work in process and conceal shortages.

### Set dynamic buffers

Buffer levels should reflect:

- Consumption variability
- Supplier reliability
- Replenishment time
- Consequence of shortage
- Shelf-life or obsolescence exposure

Inventory should be added selectively where its carrying and obsolescence cost is lower than the margin lost through long lead times.

---

## 3.4 Supplier changes

For critical suppliers:

- Measure confirmed versus actual delivery by part and purchase order.
- Share a rolling 12- or 16-week demand signal.
- Place blanket orders with scheduled releases for common components.
- Establish supplier capacity reservations where justified.
- Develop approved second sources for high-risk components.
- Negotiate smaller, more frequent deliveries.
- Use vendor-managed inventory or consignment for suitable items.
- Preapprove material substitutions through engineering and quality.
- Require advance notice of process or material changes.
- Introduce supplier corrective action for recurring defects.
- Conduct source inspection for selected critical components when it prevents a later queue.
- Certify capable suppliers so incoming inspection can be reduced based on evidence and applicable standards.

Reducing incoming inspection must be risk-based and permitted by the quality system. It should follow demonstrated supplier capability, not precede it.

---

# 4. Protect and improve certified quality gates

The quality gates should remain. The waiting around them and the defects arriving at them can be reduced.

## 4.1 Define each gate explicitly

For every certified inspection, document:

- Applicable standard or regulation
- Required records and traceability
- Entry criteria
- Inspection or test method
- Sampling plan, where permitted
- Authorized inspector qualifications
- Independence requirements
- Acceptance criteria
- Expected duration
- Escalation path for nonconformance
- Customer or third-party witness requirements

This separates mandatory controls from inherited practices that may no longer add value.

---

## 4.2 Schedule inspections as operations

Inspection should appear in the finite-capacity production schedule, with:

- A planned time slot
- Named or qualified resource pool
- Advance notification
- Complete inspection package
- Calibrated tools and fixtures
- Material and component traceability
- Contingency capacity for absence or demand peaks

Production should not complete an operation and then ask quality to “fit it in.” Quality should see the expected inspection demand before the shift or week begins.

Cross-train and certify additional inspectors where regulations and accreditation rules allow. Maintain independence where required; cross-training is not permission for operators to approve their own work.

---

## 4.3 Build quality into the operation

Before each formal gate:

- Operators perform documented self-checks.
- Critical parameters are captured automatically where practical.
- Fixtures and mistake-proofing prevent incorrect assembly.
- Tools have current calibration status.
- Electronic travelers verify material, process, and operator authorization.
- Statistical process control identifies drift before final inspection.
- Layered process audits test adherence to standard work.
- First-piece verification is used after setup or changeover.

This should reduce the number of failures reaching certified inspection without diluting the inspection itself.

---

## 4.4 Accelerate nonconformance resolution

A defect can take minutes to detect and days to disposition. Introduce:

- Immediate digital nonconformance creation
- Clear severity and containment rules
- A daily rapid-review board involving quality, engineering, and production
- Preapproved disposition rules for recurring low-risk conditions where standards allow
- Defined response times for engineering decisions
- Material review board availability within hours rather than days
- Root-cause and corrective-action requirements for recurring defects

No informal “use as is” decisions should be permitted. Faster disposition should mean quicker qualified decisions, not weaker ones.

---

## 4.5 Maintain an explicit quality firewall

During the improvement program:

- No mandatory inspection may be removed without formal quality and regulatory approval.
- No shipment may occur with incomplete certified records.
- No inspection result may be overridden to meet a delivery date.
- Inspector independence and qualification requirements remain unchanged.
- Any process change affecting form, fit, function, safety, or certification follows formal change control.
- Warranty and field-performance data are reviewed by product family and change cohort.

This firewall should be visible to customers and employees. It helps distinguish the current effort from the previous schedule-compression attempt.

---

# 5. Pilot before broad implementation

Choose one product family representing meaningful sales volume with:

- Repeated designs
- Reasonably stable demand
- A manageable set of suppliers
- Material commonality
- Known inspection requirements
- Material exposure to delivery-related lost sales

Do not start with the easiest low-volume product merely to produce an attractive result.

## Pilot design

Create a dedicated cross-functional value-stream team with authority over:

- Order qualification
- Engineering release
- Material allocation
- Scheduling
- Production flow
- Quality planning
- Supplier escalation
- Shipment readiness

For the first pilot orders:

1. Confirm complete specifications before acceptance.
2. Reserve materials and bottleneck capacity.
3. Schedule every inspection gate in advance.
4. Use standard work and controlled transfer batches.
5. Hold daily 15-minute order-flow reviews.
6. Escalate abnormalities immediately.
7. Record every hour of waiting and its cause.
8. Compare warranty and first-pass yield with the historical baseline.

The pilot should run through enough orders to encounter normal variability. A handful of executive-expedited units would not establish a repeatable six-week capability.

---

# 6. Align sales, production, and quality

The three functions are likely optimizing different outcomes:

- Sales: earliest possible promise and maximum order acceptance
- Production: stable schedules, long runs, and high resource utilization
- Quality: conformity, traceability, and independence

None of these objectives is unreasonable. Taken separately, however, they can produce a 14-week lead time.

## 6.1 Give the team a shared objective

Use one value-stream scorecard:

| Outcome | Shared metric |
|---|---|
| Customer promise | Quoted lead time by product lane |
| Reliability | On-time delivery to original promise |
| Flow | Median and 90th-percentile order-to-ship time |
| Quality | First-pass yield at each certified gate |
| Customer protection | Warranty claims and field failures |
| Stability | Schedule changes inside frozen window |
| Material readiness | Orders released with complete kits |
| Commercial result | Win rate and margin in delivery-sensitive deals |
| Compliance | Certification or audit findings |
| Improvement | Queue time removed without gate bypass |

Bonuses and recognition should not reward sales for bookings, production for utilization, or quality for hold avoidance in isolation.

---

## 6.2 Establish joint decision rights

A small value-stream leadership group should include:

- Sales or product-line leader
- Production leader
- Quality leader
- Engineering representative
- Supply-chain representative
- Finance or analytics support

Suggested decision rights:

- **Sales** owns complete customer requirements and use of approved lead-time lanes.
- **Operations** owns the executable schedule and production flow.
- **Quality** owns conformity, gate design, inspector qualification, and release authority.
- **Engineering** owns controlled product and process changes.
- **Supply chain** owns material availability and supplier recovery.
- **The value-stream leader** resolves cross-functional trade-offs within agreed safety, quality, capacity, and margin boundaries.

Quality retains independent stop-ship authority. The value-stream leader should not be able to overrule a certification failure.

---

## 6.3 Replace blame meetings with order-flow reviews

A brief daily meeting should review exceptions:

- Orders at risk
- Material shortages
- Engineering questions
- Inspection demand for the next several days
- Nonconformances awaiting disposition
- Capacity constraints
- Requested schedule changes

The language could remain factual:

- “Where is the order waiting?”
- “What entry condition is missing?”
- “Who has the next action, and by when?”
- “Is this a recurring system condition?”
- “What would prevent it on the next order?”

Functional performance reviews can continue separately. The lead-time meeting should concern flow, not departmental defense.

---

## 6.4 Create a no-fault baseline period

For the first 30 days, delay data should be used to identify the system rather than assign individual fault, except in cases of misconduct or deliberate control bypass. Otherwise, timestamps and causes may become contested or quietly reclassified.

After the baseline is established, ownership and service levels can become more explicit.

---

# 7. Implementation roadmap

## Days 0–30: Establish facts and immediate controls

- Name a value-stream leader.
- Map elapsed time for recent orders.
- Segment products into standard, configured, and engineered lanes.
- Identify the actual capacity constraint.
- Measure inspection queue time separately from inspection duration.
- Freeze quality gates and prohibit informal bypasses.
- Introduce daily order-flow reviews.
- Stop releasing jobs with missing critical material or documentation.
- Give sales an interim lead-time matrix rather than one universal promise.
- Start monitoring warranty, first-pass yield, and nonconformances by order cohort.

### Day-30 output

- Factual 14-week lead-time bridge
- Top five delay causes quantified
- Pilot product family selected
- Quality-gate map approved
- Baseline metrics agreed across functions
- Initial fast-lane criteria defined

---

## Days 31–90: Pilot a 9–10-week flow

- Create preapproved configurations and complete-order rules.
- Introduce finite-capacity scheduling at the constraint.
- Establish a frozen scheduling window.
- Schedule quality inspections in advance.
- Cross-train or add inspection capacity where queues justify it.
- Build complete material kits.
- Place targeted buffers on long-lead common components.
- Reduce transfer batches and setup time.
- Launch rapid nonconformance disposition.
- Secure supplier delivery commitments.
- Quote shorter lead times only for pilot-eligible orders.

### Month-3 gate

Proceed if the pilot demonstrates:

- Material reduction in median and 90th-percentile lead time
- No deterioration in first-pass yield
- No missed certified inspections
- Stable or improved warranty indicators
- Higher on-time delivery
- Repeatability without executive expediting

---

## Months 4–6: Reach 7–8 weeks for the selected family

- Expand product and process standardization.
- Introduce postponement and modular subassemblies.
- Establish supplier agreements and second sources.
- Reconfigure flow into product-family cells where justified.
- Digitize inspection requests and certification records.
- Balance bottleneck production, test, and inspection capacity.
- Update sales incentives around feasible promises and contribution margin.
- Extend the fast lane to adjacent configurations only after capability is demonstrated.

### Month-6 gate

A 7–8-week quote should be authorized where:

- At least 80–90% of eligible orders meet the proposed lead time
- The 90th-percentile result supports the promise
- First-pass yield is at or above baseline
- Warranty and field-failure rates show no adverse trend
- Material availability is supported by stable replenishment policies
- Quality capacity is planned rather than expedited
- The result survives normal demand, absence, and supplier variability

---

## Months 7–12: Approach six weeks selectively

- Extend the model across suitable product families.
- Refine capable-to-promise rules using live capacity and material data.
- Reduce remaining engineering and approval queues.
- Deepen supplier integration.
- Automate traceability and test-data collection where economically justified.
- Adjust buffers based on actual consumption and reliability.
- Continue design-for-manufacture and modularization work.
- Retain longer promises for genuinely engineered and high-risk products.

The six-week quote should become a standard operating capability for defined products, not a sales exception.

---

# 8. Scorecard and safeguards

| Dimension | Metric | Suggested direction |
|---|---|---|
| Lead time | Median order-to-ship time | Reduce progressively toward 6–8 weeks |
| Reliability | 90th-percentile lead time | Close enough to support the quoted promise |
| Delivery | On-time to original customer promise | Above 90%, then toward 95%+ |
| Flow | Queue time as percentage of total lead time | Sustained reduction |
| Quality | First-pass yield at certified gates | No deterioration; improve |
| Field quality | Warranty claims by production cohort | No adverse increase |
| Compliance | Mandatory gates completed correctly | 100% |
| Documentation | Complete certification pack at shipment | 100% |
| Schedule stability | Changes inside frozen window | Declining |
| Materials | Complete-kit availability at release | Above 95% for fast-lane orders |
| Suppliers | On-time delivery for critical components | Sustained improvement |
| Commercial | Deals lost solely on delivery | Material reduction |
| Forecasting | Quoted versus actual lead time | Within agreed tolerance |
| Expediting | Orders requiring executive intervention | Declining toward zero |

Warranty is a lagging indicator, so early safeguards should also include first-pass yield, process-capability measures, audit results, defect escape rates, and nonconformance recurrence.

---

# Recommended management position

The company might frame the effort this way:

> The objective is not to make certified work move faster by asking people to hurry. It is to ensure that complete orders, available materials, qualified capacity, and scheduled inspections arrive together.

Production, sales, and quality should be jointly accountable for a reliable customer promise, while quality retains independent authority over certification and release. A product-family pilot can establish a shorter lead time without repeating the warranty failure. If the data confirm that most of the 14 weeks is queue and coordination time, a 7–8-week offer should be achievable relatively quickly, with a selective six-week lane following after the process proves stable.

6. **Use standard work and takt-based balancing.**  
   Document the sequence, expected duration, quality checks, and escalation route for each operation.

7. **Apply quick-changeover methods.**  
   Externalize setup tasks, pre-stage tools, and standardize fixtures to make smaller batches economically practical.

8. **Protect bottleneck uptime.**  
   Prioritize preventive maintenance, trained backup operators, tool availability, and material kits at the constraint.

9. **Stop indiscriminate expediting.**  
   Track every override. Expedites often appear to help the selected customer while lengthening average lead time and increasing errors.

The objective is controlled, visible flow—not maximum local utilization. A machine or inspector occasionally waiting may be less costly than every order waiting.

---

## 3.3 Material and inventory strategy

A six-week customer lead time is difficult if critical components have eight- or twelve-week replenishment times. Some risk may need to be moved from customer lead time into carefully chosen inventory or supplier commitments.

### Inventory segmentation

Classify components by:

- Supplier lead time
- Demand frequency and predictability
- Commonality across products
- Unit value
- Obsolescence risk
- Quality criticality
- Supply disruption risk

Use different policies:

### Stock common, stable components

Hold controlled buffers for high-usage items shared across product families, particularly where supplier lead time exceeds the customer promise.

### Postpone configuration

Stock generic platforms, frames, housings, control modules, or semi-finished assemblies and add customer-specific features after order receipt.

### Avoid speculative stock for unique items

Continue purchasing rare or expensive engineered components to order, and quote those products accordingly.

### Create complete material kits

Do not release an order to production unless critical materials, approved substitutes, drawings, tooling, and inspection plans are available. Partial starts usually inflate work in process and conceal shortages.

### Set dynamic buffers

Buffer levels should reflect:

- Consumption variability
- Supplier reliability
- Replenishment time
- Consequence of shortage
- Shelf-life or obsolescence exposure

Inventory should be added selectively where its carrying and obsolescence cost is lower than the margin lost through long lead times.

---

## 3.4 Supplier changes

For critical suppliers:

- Measure confirmed versus actual delivery by part and purchase order.
- Share a rolling 12- or 16-week demand signal.
- Place blanket orders with scheduled releases for common components.
- Establish supplier capacity reservations where justified.
- Develop approved second sources for high-risk components.
- Negotiate smaller, more frequent deliveries.
- Use vendor-managed inventory or consignment for suitable items.
- Preapprove material substitutions through engineering and quality.
- Require advance notice of process or material changes.
- Introduce supplier corrective action for recurring defects.
- Conduct source inspection for selected critical components when it prevents a later queue.
- Certify capable suppliers so incoming inspection can be reduced based on evidence and applicable standards.

Reducing incoming inspection must be risk-based and permitted by the quality system. It should follow demonstrated supplier capability, not precede it.

---

# 4. Protect and improve certified quality gates

The quality gates should remain. The waiting around them and the defects arriving at them can be reduced.

## 4.1 Define each gate explicitly

For every certified inspection, document:

- Applicable standard or regulation
- Required records and traceability
- Entry criteria
- Inspection or test method
- Sampling plan, where permitted
- Authorized inspector qualifications
- Independence requirements
- Acceptance criteria
- Expected duration
- Escalation path for nonconformance
- Customer or third-party witness requirements

This separates mandatory controls from inherited practices that may no longer add value.

---

## 4.2 Schedule inspections as operations

Inspection should appear in the finite-capacity production schedule, with:

- A planned time slot
- Named or qualified resource pool
- Advance notification
- Complete inspection package
- Calibrated tools and fixtures
- Material and component traceability
- Contingency capacity for absence or demand peaks

Production should not complete an operation and then ask quality to “fit it in.” Quality should see the expected inspection demand before the shift or week begins.

Cross-train and certify additional inspectors where regulations and accreditation rules allow. Maintain independence where required; cross-training is not permission for operators to approve their own work.

---

## 4.3 Build quality into the operation

Before each formal gate:

- Operators perform documented self-checks.
- Critical parameters are captured automatically where practical.
- Fixtures and mistake-proofing prevent incorrect assembly.
- Tools have current calibration status.
- Electronic travelers verify material, process, and operator authorization.
- Statistical process control identifies drift before final inspection.
- Layered process audits test adherence to standard work.
- First-piece verification is used after setup or changeover.

This should reduce the number of failures reaching certified inspection without diluting the inspection itself.

---

## 4.4 Accelerate nonconformance resolution

A defect can take minutes to detect and days to disposition. Introduce:

- Immediate digital nonconformance creation
- Clear severity and containment rules
- A daily rapid-review board involving quality, engineering, and production
- Preapproved disposition rules for recurring low-risk conditions where standards allow
- Defined response times for engineering decisions
- Material review board availability within hours rather than days
- Root-cause and corrective-action requirements for recurring defects

No informal “use as is” decisions should be permitted. Faster disposition should mean quicker qualified decisions, not weaker ones.

---

## 4.5 Maintain an explicit quality firewall

During the improvement program:

- No mandatory inspection may be removed without formal quality and regulatory approval.
- No shipment may occur with incomplete certified records.
- No inspection result may be overridden to meet a delivery date.
- Inspector independence and qualification requirements remain unchanged.
- Any process change affecting form, fit, function, safety, or certification follows formal change control.
- Warranty and field-performance data are reviewed by product family and change cohort.

This firewall should be visible to customers and employees. It helps distinguish the current effort from the previous schedule-compression attempt.

---

# 5. Pilot before broad implementation

Choose one product family representing meaningful sales volume with:

- Repeated designs
- Reasonably stable demand
- A manageable set of suppliers
- Material commonality
- Known inspection requirements
- Material exposure to delivery-related lost sales

Do not start with the easiest low-volume product merely to produce an attractive result.

## Pilot design

Create a dedicated cross-functional value-stream team with authority over:

- Order qualification
- Engineering release
- Material allocation
- Scheduling
- Production flow
- Quality planning
- Supplier escalation
- Shipment readiness

For the first pilot orders:

1. Confirm complete specifications before acceptance.
2. Reserve materials and bottleneck capacity.
3. Schedule every inspection gate in advance.
4. Use standard work and controlled transfer batches.
5. Hold daily 15-minute order-flow reviews.
6. Escalate abnormalities immediately.
7. Record every hour of waiting and its cause.
8. Compare warranty and first-pass yield with the historical baseline.

The pilot should run through enough orders to encounter normal variability. A handful of executive-expedited units would not establish a repeatable six-week capability.

---

# 6. Align sales, production, and quality

The three functions are likely optimizing different outcomes:

- Sales: earliest possible promise and maximum order acceptance
- Production: stable schedules, long runs, and high resource utilization
- Quality: conformity, traceability, and independence

None of these objectives is unreasonable. Taken separately, however, they can produce a 14-week lead time.

## 6.1 Give the team a shared objective

Use one value-stream scorecard:

| Outcome | Shared metric |
|---|---|
| Customer promise | Quoted lead time by product lane |
| Reliability | On-time delivery to original promise |
| Flow | Median and 90th-percentile order-to-ship time |
| Quality | First-pass yield at each certified gate |
| Customer protection | Warranty claims and field failures |
| Stability | Schedule changes inside frozen window |
| Material readiness | Orders released with complete kits |
| Commercial result | Win rate and margin in delivery-sensitive deals |
| Compliance | Certification or audit findings |
| Improvement | Queue time removed without gate bypass |

Bonuses and recognition should not reward sales for bookings, production for utilization, or quality for hold avoidance in isolation.

---

## 6.2 Establish joint decision rights

A small value-stream leadership group should include:

- Sales or product-line leader
- Production leader
- Quality leader
- Engineering representative
- Supply-chain representative
- Finance or analytics support

Suggested decision rights:

- **Sales** owns complete customer requirements and use of approved lead-time lanes.
- **Operations** owns the executable schedule and production flow.
- **Quality** owns conformity, gate design, inspector qualification, and release authority.
- **Engineering** owns controlled product and process changes.
- **Supply chain** owns material availability and supplier recovery.
- **The value-stream leader** resolves cross-functional trade-offs within agreed safety, quality, capacity, and margin boundaries.

Quality retains independent stop-ship authority. The value-stream leader should not be able to overrule a certification failure.

---

## 6.3 Replace blame meetings with order-flow reviews

A brief daily meeting should review exceptions:

- Orders at risk
- Material shortages
- Engineering questions
- Inspection demand for the next several days
- Nonconformances awaiting disposition
- Capacity constraints
- Requested schedule changes

The language could remain factual:

- “Where is the order waiting?”
- “What entry condition is missing?”
- “Who has the next action, and by when?”
- “Is this a recurring system condition?”
- “What would prevent it on the next order?”

Functional performance reviews can continue separately. The lead-time meeting should concern flow, not departmental defense.

---

## 6.4 Create a no-fault baseline period

For the first 30 days, delay data should be used to identify the system rather than assign individual fault, except in cases of misconduct or deliberate control bypass. Otherwise, timestamps and causes may become contested or quietly reclassified.

After the baseline is established, ownership and service levels can become more explicit.

---

# 7. Implementation roadmap

## Days 0–30: Establish facts and immediate controls

- Name a value-stream leader.
- Map elapsed time for recent orders.
- Segment products into standard, configured, and engineered lanes.
- Identify the actual capacity constraint.
- Measure inspection queue time separately from inspection duration.
- Freeze quality gates and prohibit informal bypasses.
- Introduce daily order-flow reviews.
- Stop releasing jobs with missing critical material or documentation.
- Give sales an interim lead-time matrix rather than one universal promise.
- Start monitoring warranty, first-pass yield, and nonconformances by order cohort.

### Day-30 output

- Factual 14-week lead-time bridge
- Top five delay causes quantified
- Pilot product family selected
- Quality-gate map approved
- Baseline metrics agreed across functions
- Initial fast-lane criteria defined

---

## Days 31–90: Pilot a 9–10-week flow

- Create preapproved configurations and complete-order rules.
- Introduce finite-capacity scheduling at the constraint.
- Establish a frozen scheduling window.
- Schedule quality inspections in advance.
- Cross-train or add inspection capacity where queues justify it.
- Build complete material kits.
- Place targeted buffers on long-lead common components.
- Reduce transfer batches and setup time.
- Launch rapid nonconformance disposition.
- Secure supplier delivery commitments.
- Quote shorter lead times only for pilot-eligible orders.

### Month-3 gate

Proceed if the pilot demonstrates:

- Material reduction in median and 90th-percentile lead time
- No deterioration in first-pass yield
- No missed certified inspections
- Stable or improved warranty indicators
- Higher on-time delivery
- Repeatability without executive expediting

---

## Months 4–6: Reach 7–8 weeks for the selected family

- Expand product and process standardization.
- Introduce postponement and modular subassemblies.
- Establish supplier agreements and second sources.
- Reconfigure flow into product-family cells where justified.
- Digitize inspection requests and certification records.
- Balance bottleneck production, test, and inspection capacity.
- Update sales incentives around feasible promises and contribution margin.
- Extend the fast lane to adjacent configurations only after capability is demonstrated.

### Month-6 gate

A 7–8-week quote should be authorized where:

- At least 80–90% of eligible orders meet the proposed lead time
- The 90th-percentile result supports the promise
- First-pass yield is at or above baseline
- Warranty and field-failure rates show no adverse trend
- Material availability is supported by stable replenishment policies
- Quality capacity is planned rather than expedited
- The result survives normal demand, absence, and supplier variability

---

## Months 7–12: Approach six weeks selectively

- Extend the model across suitable product families.
- Refine capable-to-promise rules using live capacity and material data.
- Reduce remaining engineering and approval queues.
- Deepen supplier integration.
- Automate traceability and test-data collection where economically justified.
- Adjust buffers based on actual consumption and reliability.
- Continue design-for-manufacture and modularization work.
- Retain longer promises for genuinely engineered and high-risk products.

The six-week quote should become a standard operating capability for defined products, not a sales exception.

---

# 8. Scorecard and safeguards

| Dimension | Metric | Suggested direction |
|---|---|---|
| Lead time | Median order-to-ship time | Reduce progressively toward 6–8 weeks |
| Reliability | 90th-percentile lead time | Close enough to support the quoted promise |
| Delivery | On-time to original customer promise | Above 90%, then toward 95%+ |
| Flow | Queue time as percentage of total lead time | Sustained reduction |
| Quality | First-pass yield at certified gates | No deterioration; improve |
| Field quality | Warranty claims by production cohort | No adverse increase |
| Compliance | Mandatory gates completed correctly | 100% |
| Documentation | Complete certification pack at shipment | 100% |
| Schedule stability | Changes inside frozen window | Declining |
| Materials | Complete-kit availability at release | Above 95% for fast-lane orders |
| Suppliers | On-time delivery for critical components | Sustained improvement |
| Commercial | Deals lost solely on delivery | Material reduction |
| Forecasting | Quoted versus actual lead time | Within agreed tolerance |
| Expediting | Orders requiring executive intervention | Declining toward zero |

Warranty is a lagging indicator, so early safeguards should also include first-pass yield, process-capability measures, audit results, defect escape rates, and nonconformance recurrence.

---

# Recommended management position

The company might frame the effort this way:

> The objective is not to make certified work move faster by asking people to hurry. It is to ensure that complete orders, available materials, qualified capacity, and scheduled inspections arrive together.

Production, sales, and quality should be jointly accountable for a reliable customer promise, while quality retains independent authority over certification and release. A product-family pilot can establish a shorter lead time without repeating the warranty failure. If the data confirm that most of the 14 weeks is queue and coordination time, a 7–8-week offer should be achievable relatively quickly, with a selective six-week lane following after the process proves stable.
